"""
"""
Purpose  
To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance (QA).

Materials and Methods  

Overview of Workflow  
This retrospective study assessed a two-stage AI pipeline for structuring and QA of radiology reports. The system first segmented reports into anatomical sections using a rule-based agent, then refined assignments and performed QA tasks using a local large language model (LLM) agent. Performance was evaluated by radiologist review of a stratified sample of reports.

Study Design, Data, and Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria  
A total of 638 radiology reports from CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis exams, dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists at a single institution in 2023–2024, were included. Inclusion criteria: finalized (not preliminary) reports for adult patients (age ≥18 years) from routine CT chest, abdomen, and/or pelvis exams. Exclusion criteria: addenda, preliminary or draft reports, pediatric cases, and studies with incomplete metadata or missing sections. Reports were identified from the institutional PACS.

Sampling and Stratification  
Reports were randomly sampled using a stratified approach to ensure representativeness by exam type (chest, abdomen, pelvis, or combination), reporting radiologist, and report length (short, medium, long tertiles by sentence count). Stratification hierarchy was: (1) exam type, (2) radiologist within exam type, (3) report length within radiologist group. If a report qualified for multiple strata, assignment followed this order. In cases of overlap or insufficient numbers, random selection was used to fill remaining slots, maintaining proportional representation. The final evaluation set of 45 reports included 23 flagged and 22 unflagged reports, reflecting the overall flagged/unflagged ratio. Table 1 summarizes the sampling process and final strata composition. Potential biases include overrepresentation of certain exam types or radiologists if strata were small, and the single-institution, retrospective design.

Table 1. Stratified Sampling Summary  
| Exam Type      | Radiologists | Short | Medium | Long | Total |
|----------------|-------------|-------|--------|------|-------|
| Chest          | 5           | 3     | 3      | 3    | 9     |
| Abdomen        | 5           | 3     | 3      | 3    | 9     |
| Pelvis         | 2           | 2     | 2      | 2    | 6     |
| Combo (C/A/P)  | 3           | 3     | 3      | 3    | 9     |
| Mixed/Other    | -           | 4     | 4      | 4    | 12    |
| **Total**      | 15          | 15    | 15     | 15   | 45    |

Multi-Agent AI Pipeline Architecture  

Rule-Based Agent  
The first agent used regular expressions (regex) to identify and segment sentences into standardized anatomical sections (e.g., lungs, liver, kidneys). Regex patterns (e.g., `r"\b(lungs?|pulmonary)\b"`, `r"\b(liver|hepatic)\b"`) were iteratively developed by reviewing 100 randomly selected local reports. The final set included 18 anatomical section patterns. Patterns were refined to maximize recall (target >95%) and minimize false positives (target <5%), as measured by manual review on a validation set of 50 reports. On this set, the regex agent achieved recall of 96.2% and precision of 94.8%. These thresholds were based on prior studies (e.g., Johnson et al., J Digit Imaging 2019;32:567–575) and internal pilot data showing that recall below 95% led to frequent omission of important findings.

LLM Agent and Prompt Engineering  
A 7B-parameter Llama-2 model, running on-premises, was used to resolve ambiguous assignments and perform semantic QA checks. The LLM was prompted with institution-specific instructions. Prompt engineering involved 5 major iterations, each tested on a validation set of 30 reports. The final prompt achieved 92.3% agreement with expert assignments (Cohen’s kappa = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81–0.95). The >90% agreement threshold was chosen to ensure high reliability and minimize clinically significant misassignments, consistent with standards in prior NLP studies (e.g., Pons et al., Radiology 2016;279:329–343).

Agent Interaction and QA Tasks  
A controller script orchestrated the pipeline: the regex agent generated preliminary section assignments, which the LLM agent reviewed and refined. The LLM also performed three QA tasks using prompt-based logic:  
(a) Section mismatch: “Are there findings in the Findings section not reflected in the Impression, or vice versa?”  
(b) Gender-anatomy conflict: “Does the report mention anatomical findings inconsistent with the patient’s gender?”  
(c) Undocumented critical findings: “Is there mention of a critical finding, and if so, is communication documented?”  
Prompts for each task were validated by comparing LLM outputs to expert annotations on 50 reports. Final error rates were: section mismatch (false positive 6%, false negative 8%), gender-anatomy conflict (false positive 2%, false negative 4%), undocumented critical findings (false positive 8%, false negative 6%). These thresholds (<10%) were set to balance sensitivity and specificity, minimizing missed critical findings while avoiding excessive false alarms, in line with published QA tool standards (e.g., Langlotz et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2017;14:1180–1186).

Primary and Secondary Outcomes  
Primary outcome: correct restructuring rate, defined as the proportion of reports in which all sentences were assigned to the correct anatomical section with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information.  
Secondary outcomes: (1) performance of each QA task (sensitivity, specificity, false positive/negative rates), (2) inter-rater reliability (Cohen’s kappa), (3) frequency and nature of reviewer disagreements, and (4) system inference time and hardware requirements.

Evaluation Criteria, Inter-Rater Reliability, and Consensus  
Correctness of restructuring was defined as all sentences assigned to correct anatomical sections, with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information (operationalized as findings that could alter patient management, e.g., new or significant lesions, critical findings, actionable findings per ACR guidelines). Two board-certified radiologists independently assessed:  
(1) Correctness of restructuring,  
(2) QA task performance—each flagged issue rated as true/false positive/negative,  
(3) Omission or fabrication of clinically important information.  
Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion. Inter-rater reliability for restructuring correctness was Cohen’s kappa = 0.74 (95% CI: 0.60–0.88), indicating substantial agreement. Of 45 reports, 12 (27%) had initial disagreement: 8 involved borderline section assignments, 3 involved omission of minor findings, 1 involved ambiguous language. Consensus was achieved in all cases. The impact of disagreements is that borderline or ambiguous cases may be subject to interpretation, potentially affecting measured accuracy.

Statistical Analysis  
All statistical analyses were performed using Python 3.10 with SciPy and statsmodels. Proportions and confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the Wilson score method. Cohen’s kappa was used to assess inter-rater reliability, interpreted as: 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81–1.00 almost perfect agreement. For QA task performance, sensitivity, specificity, and 95% CIs were calculated. No missing data were present. Power analysis for the primary outcome was performed using the statsmodels “power” module, assuming a binomial distribution.

System Requirements and Deployment  
The system was deployed on a workstation with dual NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, and Ubuntu 22.04. LLM inference averaged 2.5 seconds per report; regex processing was <0.1 seconds per report. On a standard clinical workstation (Intel Xeon CPU, 64 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU), LLM inference time increased to 12.8 seconds per report. Model quantization and use of smaller models (e.g., 3B-parameter LLMs) reduced inference time by 40–60% with minimal loss in accuracy (<2% drop in agreement). The system operated as a standalone batch processor and was not integrated into clinical workflow. Integration challenges include PACS/RIS compatibility, user interface development, and real-time feedback. Barriers to deployment include IT security, workflow disruption, and user training. Steps needed for real-world adoption include API development, EHR integration, and prospective pilot testing.

Results  

Primary Outcome: Report Structuring  
The system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format, retaining original content. Of the 45 evaluated reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and 12 (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%) had initial reviewer disagreement (resolved by consensus). No clinically important information was omitted or fabricated in correctly restructured reports. Table 2 summarizes restructuring outcomes.
